To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i): during coevolution, the bacterial biocontrol pathogen Bacillus thuringienisis evolves high virulence to its nematode prey host Caenorhabdities elegans, which is associated with increased copy number of the plasmids that contain the toxin genes; (ii): the toxin genes and plasmid are not required for the pathogen to survive in the absence of the host, but are necessary for the pathogen's high virulence to the host; and

the bacterial biocontrol pathogen Bacillus thuringienisis has a high virulence towards nematodes that is mediated by toxin genes located on plasmids, that this pathogen can adapt to the nematode host during coevolution, that the toxin genes are specifically involved in the adaptation process, and that the virulence of the toxin genes is essential for the adaptation.

(i): high virulence was favoured in the pathogen during coevolution with its nematode prey; (ii) this was due to a selective sweep of a pathogen strain that carried a plasmid with nematocidal Cry toxin genes; and (iii) the toxin genes were necessary for high virulence in a strain lacking the toxin plasmid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a pathogen–host interaction system that is a natural model for the study of rapid adaptation and coevolution.
the genetic basis of coevolution between a pathogen and its host, which is mediated by the dynamics of virulence genes.
the evolution of pathogen virulences and the genetic and functional mechanisms that underlie the rapid adaptation process in the context of coevolutionary dynamics.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
coevolution with the host is an important selective pressure on the pathogen's virulence and that this selection is mediated by toxin genes.
our results demonstrate the selective advantage of pathogen virulency and its toxin genes during host-pathogen coevolution.
coevolution is not only a driver of evolution but also a mechanism for the emergence of novel genes, gene functions and life history strategies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified the genetic basis of coevolutionary fitness in an experimental model system.
we demonstrate the selective advantage of pathogen virulent and its Cry toxin genes during the host–pathogen coevolution.
we have shown that the pathogen's toxin genes and virulence are adaptive traits in its coevolution with its host and that virulence is maintained by natural selection in the pathogen genome.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the spatiotemporal dynamics of interaction between host and pathogenic microorganisms may substantially influence the process of host–pathogen coevolution and result in surprising evolutionary outcomes.
the pathogen's capacity to generate and employ adaptive toxins in combination with high virulence may represent a powerful weapon in its coevolutionary interactions with hosts.
, in line with theoretical prediction, coevolution is a dynamic and continuously adaptive process that enables contrasting host and pathogen phenotypes with subsequent diversifying selection.
